In other instances, though, such as the 12A and 8B groups, the hemilineage cluster is more complex and contains obvious subclasses of interneurons.
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical observations.

claims.claim: The more homogenous hemilineages are likely collections of parallel components providing parallel but overlapping channels in sensory to motor transformation circuits.
claims.source: We speculate that the more homogenous hemilineages are collections of parallel components, which provide parallel but overlapping channels in the circuits that control sensory to motor transformations.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the anatomical observations.

claims.claim: The more heterogeneous hemilineages likely have more diversified integrative functions.
claims.source: The more heterogeneous hemilineages likely have more diversified integrative functions.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the anatomical observations.

claims.claim: Many brain lineages in Drosophila contain a greater diversity of cell types than VNS hemilineages.
claims.source: The recent characterization of lineages in the fly brain (Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013) shows many brain lineages that contain a greater diversity of cell types than we see for the VNS hemilineages.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Some brain lineages appear to be simple, rather homogeneous collections of neurons that represent parallel processing units.
claims.source: Nevertheless, some of the brain lineages also appear to be simple, rather homogeneous collections of neurons and we would expect these to also represent parallel processing units.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with VNS hemilineages and brain lineage data.

claims.claim: A projection neuron hemilineage from the lateral antennal lobe (lAL) NB contains five classes of projection neurons all involved in receiving primary sensory input and relaying it to higher centers.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: Most hemilineage lines had some degree of contamination with expression in neurons outside of the target hemilineage.
claims.source: As summarized in Supplementary file 1, most of our lines had some degree of contamination with expression in neurons that were outside of our target hemilineage.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the experimental limitations of the study.

claims.claim: Lines showing expression in sensory neurons (such as hemilineages 3A and 19B) were not used for behavioral studies.
claims.source: We did not use lines that showed expression in sensory neurons (such as hemilineages 3A and 19B), or that had expression in other hemilineage clusters (e.g., the hemilineage 14A line).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about experimental methodology.

claims.claim: Decapitated flies showed a complex array of behaviors during the tests despite lacking their heads.
claims.source: Despite lacking their heads, these flies showed a complex array of behaviors during the tests.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments.

claims.claim: Tonic responses were more common than sequential responses during TRPA1 activation.
claims.source: Tonic responses were the more common and are defined as a persistent behavioral response that began at some point during the heat ramp and were then maintained for the remainder of the stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of behavioral observations.

claims.claim: Stimulation of 12A neurons caused decapitated flies to display an ordered sequence of behavioral responses that changed as temperature increased.
claims.source: This was very evident for the stimulation of the 12A neurons that began with locomotion that was later joined by lateral wing waving and then finally by the onset of sustained wing buzzing.
claims.evidence: This is a description of behavioral observations.

claims.claim: The 9A and 5B clusters are GABA-immunopositive neurons.
claims.source: We do not have detailed transmitter information for all of the hemilineage groups but we do know that the 9A and 5B clusters are GABA-immunopositive neurons (Harris, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: For hemilineages that evoked more complex behaviors, the response to stimulation was probabilistic rather than deterministic.
claims.source: The hemilineages that evoked more complex behaviors typically showed a range of behaviors, although there was usually a dominant category of response that characterized that particular hemilineage group. Therefore, for these more complex behaviors, the response to hemilineage group stimulation was probabilistic rather than deterministic, in that the activity of these neurons enhanced the probability that a particular behavior would be performed.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from behavioral observations.

claims.claim: Larval Drosophila behavioral responses to TRPA1 activation of different sparse sets of central neurons tended to be probabilistic.
claims.source: A similar phenomenon was seen in the behavioral responses of larval Drosophila to TRPA1 activation of different sparse sets of central neurons (Vogelstein et al., 2014). The larval behavioral responses also tended to be probabilistic in that a given set of neurons enhanced the probability of a behavioral response but their activity did not invariably lead to this response.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: Hemilineage groups that evoke changes in leg posture have their arbors concentrated in the leg neuropils.
claims.source: Not surprisingly, the hemilineage groups that evoke changes in leg posture have their arbors concentrated in the leg neuropils.
claims.evidence: This is a correlation between anatomical and behavioral data shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Hemilineages that evoke coordinated or uncoordinated leg movements have a strong leg neuropil component but their arbors also project into the medial neuropil and into the tectulum neuropil.
claims.source: Hemilineages that evoke coordinated or uncoordinated leg movements similarly have a strong leg neuropil component but their arbors also project into the medial neuropil and into the tectulum neuropil.
claims.evidence: This is a correlation between anatomical and behavioral data shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Strong projections into the tectulum neuropil were evident for all hemilineages that evoked wing movements of either low or high frequency.
claims.source: Strong projections into the tectulum neuropil were also evident for all of the hemilineages that evoked wing movements of either low or high frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a correlation between anatomical and behavioral data shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Two of the three hemilineages that evoked frequent takeoff had a strong projection into the T2 leg neuropil in addition to their extensive arbor in the tectulum.
claims.source: Two of the three hemilineages that evoked frequent takeoff had a strong projection into the T2 leg neuropil (the site of the jump motoneurons) in addition to their extensive arbor in the tectulum.
claims.evidence: This is a correlation between anatomical and behavioral data shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The third takeoff lineage, lineage 11A/B, lacked a T2 arbor but had substantial projections into the T1 and T3 leg neuropils.
claims.source: Curiously, the third takeoff lineage, lineage 11A/B, lacked a T2 arbor but had substantial projections into the T1 and T3 leg neuropils.
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The leg neuropils deal with leg function while the tectulum neuropil is involved with wing-related behavior such as singing or flight.
claims.source: Overall the anatomy of the hemilineages conformed to the generally held idea that the leg neuropils deal with leg function while the tectulum neuropil is involved with wing-related behavior such as singing or flight.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from correlating anatomical and behavioral data with established knowledge.

claims.claim: The tectulum and dorsomedial neuropil may be generally involved in complex, coordinated behavior in the thorax.
claims.source: In addition, though, the tectulum and dorsomedial neuropil may be generally involved in complex, coordinated behavior in the thorax.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from anatomical and behavioral observations.

claims.claim: Hemilineages such as 1A and 10B that evoke walking behavior but little wing movement have arbor extension into the dorsomedial neuropil and tectulum.
claims.source: Hemilineages, such as 1A and 10B, that evoke walking behavior but little in the way of wing movement nevertheless have arbor extension into the dorsomedial neuropil and tectulum, suggesting that these regions may be generally involved in the coordination of complex thoracic behavior regardless of whether it involves legs or wings.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from anatomical and behavioral observations.

claims.claim: Hemilineages appear to have a modular function with cells in a given group being associated with particular behavioral responses.
claims.source: Overall the hemilineages appear to have a modular function with cells in a given group being associated with particular behavioral responses.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: In grasshoppers, computational circuits are built from clusters of distinct types of interneurons, at least some of which arise in the same lineage.
claims.source: This notion is consistent with physiological data such as that from grasshoppers in which computational circuits are built from clusters of distinct types of interneurons (Burrows, 1996), at least some types of which have been shown to arise in the same lineage (Shepherd and Laurent, 1992).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: In the vertebrate spinal cord, different cell types arise from defined sets of precursors and play specific roles in defined circuit motifs.
claims.source: A similar strategy is seen in the vertebrate spinal cord in which different cell types arise from defined sets of precursors and the neurons from those cell types play specific roles in defined circuit motifs (Grillner and Jessell, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: The vPR6 neurons are required for song production in the male.
claims.source: A second caution comes from our demonstration that the vPR6 neurons, which are required for song production in the male (von Philipsborn et al., 2011), are part of hemilineage 12A cluster (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work and data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The segmental CNS of insects provides an unparalleled system to study the evolution and diversification of the nervous system.
claims.source: The segmental CNS of insects provides an unparalleled system in which to study the evolution and diversification of the nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the advantages of the insect system.

claims.claim: The stereotyped array of segmental NBs in insects has undergone little change through the course of insect evolution.
claims.source: The advantage of the insect system lies in a stereotyped array of segmental NBs that has undergone little change through the course of insect evolution.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about insect evolution.

claims.claim: Homologous stem cells can be identified in insects as diverse as silverfish, grasshoppers and Drosophila based on position, molecular markers and early progeny.
claims.source: Based on position, molecular markers and the types of early progeny that they produce, the homologous stem cells can be identified in insects as diverse as silverfish, grasshoppers and Drosophila (Thomas et al., 1984; Truman and Ball, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The early neuronal progeny of NBs are highly conserved across insects.
claims.source: Not only have the NBs been highly conserved, but their early neuronal progeny are also highly conserved as first elegantly shown by Thomas et al. (1984).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: The early-born 'primary' neurons have identities determined by birth-order as encoded in a transcription factor progression within the cycling NB.
claims.source: These early-born cells are the 'primary' neurons and their identities are determined by birth-order as encoded in a transcription factor progression within the cycling NB (Isshiki et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: Many early-born cells serve a pioneer function, explaining the stereotyped pattern of tracts and commissures seen in the ventral neuropil throughout insects.
claims.source: Many of these early-born cells serve a pioneer function, which explains the stereotyped pattern of tracts and commissures seen in the ventral neuropil throughout the insects (Thomas et al., 1984).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: Later-born 'secondary' neurons are born after the NB starts to express grainyhead and include late-born embryonic neurons and all postembryonic neurons.
claims.source: The later-born 'secondary' neurons are born after the NB starts to express grainyhead (Almeida and Bray, 2005) and include late-born embryonic neurons as well as all of the neurons that are born during postembryonic life (see Zhou et al., 2009; for a discussion of primary vs secondary neurons).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: In grasshoppers, the medial lineage A hemilineage cells are GABAergic, engrailed-positive local interneurons and the B hemilineage cells are engrailed-negative projection cells.
claims.source: Conservation in class character in widely different groups is well illustrated by the medial lineage. In grasshoppers the A hemilineage cells are GABAergic, engrailed-positive local interneurons and the B hemilineage cells are engrailed-negative, projection cells (Jia and Siegler, 2002), and the same is true in Drosophila (JW Truman, unpublished).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work and unpublished observations.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, the medial lineage A hemilineage cells are GABAergic, engrailed-positive local interneurons and the B hemilineage cells are engrailed-negative projection cells.
claims.source: Conservation in class character in widely different groups is well illustrated by the medial lineage. claims.evidence: This is based on unpublished observations.

claims.claim: A comparative analysis of GABA-immunoreactive neurons in the VNS of diverse insects supports the contention that the properties of neurons in homologous hemilineages are highly conserved across much of the insects.
claims.source: Similarly, a comparative analysis of the clusters of GABA-immunoreactive neurons in the VNS of diverse insects (Witten and Truman, 1998) supports the contention that the properties of neurons in homologous hemilineages are highly conserved across much of the insects.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that one could homologize individual neurons within a particular class across insects.
claims.source: Although one can homologize cell classes of secondary neurons across most of the insects, we think that it is unlikely that one could homologize individual neurons within a particular class.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the authors' interpretation.

claims.claim: In grasshoppers, ventral interneurons that run in the transverse tract receive input from wing afferents.
claims.source: In grasshoppers ventral interneurons that run in the transverse tract receive input from wing afferents (Watson and Burrows, 1983) while in flies the 2A interneurons are the main neurons of the transverse tract and they can drive flight behavior.

claims.claim: In flies, the 2A interneurons are the main neurons of the transverse tract and they can drive flight behavior.

claims.claim: In grasshoppers, NB4-1 and NB3-1 make the medial and anteromedial spiking interneurons, respectively, of the leg circuit.
claims.source: For the leg hemilineages, NB4-1 and NB3-1 in grasshopper make the medial and anteromedial spiking interneurons, respectively, of the leg circuit (Burrows, 1996), while in flies the homologous NBs (Truman et al., 2004) generate the 14A and 4B interneurons which are similar appearing local interneurons in the leg neuropil.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: In flies, the homologous NBs to grasshopper NB4-1 and NB3-1 generate the 14A and 4B interneurons which are similar appearing local interneurons in the leg neuropil.
claims.source: For the leg hemilineages, NB4-1 and NB3-1 in grasshopper make the medial and anteromedial spiking interneurons, respectively, of the leg circuit (Burrows, 1996), while in flies the homologous NBs (Truman et al., 2004) generate the 14A and 4B interneurons which are similar appearing local interneurons in the leg neuropil.
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical observations and a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The functional roles of most or all of the hemilineages are expected to be highly conserved through much of insect evolution.
claims.source: We expect that the functional roles of most of all of the hemilineages to be highly conserved through much of insect evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the authors' interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: For simpler hemilineages with parallel units, addition or reduction in neuron numbers could enhance or reduce functionality by altering spatial or temporal resolution.
claims.source: For the simpler hemilineages that contain units that work in parallel, addition or reductions in the number of neurons could enhance or reduce functionality by altering the spatial or temporal resolution of their level of the computational network.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary mechanisms.

claims.claim: An increase in numbers of an interneuron type could provide finer control over the speed of locomotion, as seen for swimming speed control in larval zebrafish.

claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claims.claim: For higher level, more complex hemilineages, changes in neuronal properties/connectivity rather than numbers might be more important for generating behavioral changes.
claims.source: For higher level, more complex hemilineages, changes in neuronal properties/connectivity rather than numbers might be more important for generating behavioral changes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary mechanisms.

claims.claim: The flight system of Drosophila, with its mesothoracic wings and metathoracic halteres, is a highly derived system compared with more basal insect groups.
claims.source: It is important to remember, though, that the flight system of Drosophila, with its mesothoracic wings and metathoracic halteres, is a highly derived system compared with more basal insect groups.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about insect evolution.

claims.claim: About a third of the thoracic hemilineages die in the fly, leaving few if any members.
claims.source: Also, in the fly about a third of the thoracic hemilineages die leaving few if any members (Truman et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Some cell types that may have been important in the ancestral nervous system have been lost with the evolution of Drosophila's derived pattern of flight.

claims.claim: The analysis includes only the postembryonic secondary neurons, lacking access to the embryonic-born neurons.

claims.claim: A thoracic unit of the fly thoracic nervous system has about 2500 pairs of neurons, most of which can be assigned to 33 hemilineage units.

claims.claim: nSynaptotagmin::GFP localizes primarily in the ventral arbors of 1A neurons in the intermediate layers of the leg neuropil, showing the primary output regions of these cells.

claims.claim: Activation of 1A interneurons via TRPA1 evoked forward locomotion in decapitated flies.

claims.claim: During 1A activation, leg movements were erratic and not organized in the tripod gait typical of walking in intact flies, but there was clear intersegmental coordination of the limbs.

claims.claim: The 2A interneurons extend broadly within the ipsilateral part of the tectulum.
claims.source: This anatomy is conserved in the adult, with the 2A interneurons extending broadly within the ipsilateral part of the tectulum (Figure 4G–I).

claims.claim: Activation of the 2A interneurons drove high frequency wing movements in 54% of decapitated flies (n = 25).
claims.source: Activation of the 2A interneurons drove high frequency wing movements (54%, n = 25).

claims.claim: During 2A activation, decapitated flies typically stood in place but abruptly initiated high frequency flapping with wings extended laterally in the flight position as temperature increased.
claims.source: The decapitated flies typically stood in place but as the temperature increased, they abruptly initiated high frequency flapping with the wings extended laterally in the flight position (Figure 4J; Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral observation supported by Figure 4J and Video 3.

claims.claim: In the adult, the cell bodies of hemilineage 3A remain ventral, just posterior to the leg nerve insertion and their arbors extend through intermediate levels of the leg neuropil.

claims.claim: The cluster of 3B interneurons is severely reduced or absent in T3.

claims.claim: In T1 and T2, the arbors of 3B cells converge in the tectulum to form a complex arbor in the very dorsal layer of this neuropil.

claims.claim: Activation of 3B interneurons caused decapitated flies to show subtle repositioning of legs, repetitive poorly coordinated leg movements, occasional grooming bouts, and occasional wing flicking and scissoring movements but not high frequency wing buzzing.

claims.evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the experiments.

claims.claim: In the adult, the 5B cell bodies are pulled towards the midline and their bundled axons cross the midline in the iP commissure, forming a major ipsilateral arbor just prior to crossing.
claims.source: In the adult, the cell bodies are pulled towards the midline. Their bundled axons cross the midline in the iP commissure, and form a major ipsilateral arbor just prior to crossing (Figure 4P,Q).

claims.claim: When 5B interneurons were activated, decapitated flies showed a progressive repositioning of their limbs so that they were closer to the ground by the end of the thermal ramp.

claims.evidence: This is a behavioral observation supported by Figure 4R and Video 5.

claims.claim: Tethered intact flies gripping a Styrofoam ball responded to 5B activation by lowering their body position, drawing the ball closer to them.

claims.evidence: This is a behavioral observation supported by Figure 4S.

claims.claim: Hemilineage 6A clusters are found in neuromeres S3 through A1 and form one of the dorsalmost arbors of the tectulum.

claims.claim: nSyt::GFP localizes to the lateral portions of the contralateral arbor of 6A neurons.

claims.claim: The neurons of 6B cluster are found in T1 to T3 but typically are missing from segment A1.

claims.claim: The 6B bundle crosses in the iP commissure without an ipsilateral arbor and then branches profusely in the tectulum neuropil and the dorsal-most region of the leg neuropils.

claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Activation of 6A interneurons started with poorly coordinated leg movements that often pitched the fly forward onto its anterior thorax, followed by very erratic movements.

claims.evidence: This is a behavioral observation supported by Figure 6D and Video 6.

claims.claim: Activation of 6B interneurons in decapitated flies elicited a mixture of leg-related movements, with some showing curving forward movement while others pivoted in place.

claims.evidence: This is a behavioral observation supported by Figure 5G and Video 7.

claims.claim: The 7B neurite projects dorsally, forming a bushy ipsilateral arbor in the tectulum, then crosses the midline to form an ascending tract that extends through the neck connective.

claims.claim: The arbor of 7B neurons in the T2 hemineuromere includes prominent projections into the dorsolateral region of the T2 leg neuropil.

results.result: Drosophila thoracic neurons arise from neuroblasts through a stereotyped developmental program. Each NB divides to produce GMCs that generate A and B hemilineage daughters. In the thorax, 25 of 30 NBs generate postembryonic lineages, yielding 50 possible hemilineages, of which 17 die, leaving 33 hemilineages that account for 90-95% of adult thoracic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C17-C23 describe the developmental origin and quantitative composition of thoracic hemilineages. These claims are well-supported by citations to prior work (C18, C19) and are consistent with established knowledge about Drosophila neurogenesis. The quantitative statements (C20-C23) appear to be based on systematic anatomical analysis.

results.result: Hemilineages provide both anatomical and functional organization of the thoracic nervous system. Most hemilineages contain pools of similar interneurons, and TRPA1-mediated activation of each hemilineage elicits characteristic behavioral responses. The complexity of elicited behaviors correlates with the complexity of the hemilineage's projection pattern, suggesting a hierarchical organization where simple ventral hemilineages generate basic movements that are orchestrated by more complex dorsal hemilineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 represent the central findings of the study. The anatomical characterization (C28) is supported by systematic imaging across hemilineages. The behavioral characterization (C29) is supported by TRPA1 activation experiments across multiple hemilineages. The correlation between anatomy and behavior (C30) and the hierarchical model (C31-C32) are well-supported by the comprehensive data presented in Figures 4-9.

results.result: The study developed genetic strategies to track and manipulate hemilineages through metamorphosis. Using the Rubin GAL4 collection and temporal control methods (GeneSwitch, nSyb-GAL80), the authors could maintain larval expression patterns into adulthood and selectively target immature neurons while excluding mature neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 describe the methodological approaches. The GeneSwitch strategy (C35-C37) is demonstrated in Figure 2, showing successful temporal control. The nSyb-GAL80 approach (C38-C39) is demonstrated in Figure 3, showing selective suppression of mature neurons. These technical innovations are critical for the study and are well-documented with appropriate controls.

results.result: Larval hemilineage projections prefigure adult target regions. Seventeen hemilineages project to the leg neuropil in both larva and adult, with most showing homogeneous neuronal composition and restricted arbors. Specific hemilineages (23B, 9A) overlap with sensory afferents, while others (14A) are homologous to characterized grasshopper interneurons involved in sensorimotor transformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C48 describe the anatomical organization of leg neuropil hemilineages. The prefiguring of adult targets (C40-C41) is supported by developmental observations and citations. The sensory overlap (C45) is supported by citation to Harris 2012. The homology to grasshopper NB4-1 (C46-C48) is supported by multiple citations and anatomical similarity, providing evolutionary context.

results.result: The tectulum neuropil is built from dorsal-projecting hemilineages that converge on T2 during metamorphosis. Some tectulum hemilineages (6A, 6B) are relatively homogeneous, while others (12A, 8B) contain obvious subclasses. The authors speculate that homogeneous hemilineages provide parallel processing channels while heterogeneous ones have more diversified integrative functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 describe anatomical observations that are well-supported by the imaging data. However, C52-C53 are explicitly speculative interpretations about functional roles. While the speculation is reasonable given the anatomical diversity, it lacks direct experimental support. The functional claims would require additional experiments such as selective manipulation of subpopulations within heterogeneous hemilineages.

results.result: Decapitated flies showed complex behaviors during TRPA1 activation experiments. Behavioral responses were predominantly tonic (sustained) rather than sequential, though some hemilineages (e.g., 12A) showed ordered behavioral sequences. For complex behaviors, responses were probabilistic rather than deterministic, similar to observations in larval Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 describe general features of the behavioral responses. The observation of complex behaviors in decapitated flies (C59) is well-documented across multiple videos. The distinction between tonic and sequential responses (C60-C61) is clearly illustrated (e.g., Figure 6J for 12A). The probabilistic nature of complex behaviors (C63) is a reasonable interpretation supported by the variability observed across trials, and is consistent with prior work (C64, citation to Vogelstein et al. 2014).

results.result: Hemilineage anatomy correlates with behavioral function. Hemilineages evoking leg posture changes project to leg neuropils; those evoking coordinated movements project to both leg and tectulum neuropils; those evoking wing movements project strongly to tectulum. The tectulum and dorsomedial neuropil may be generally involved in coordinating complex thoracic behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C72 describe structure-function relationships summarized in Figure 9. The correlations between projection patterns and behavioral outputs (C65-C69) are well-supported by the comprehensive anatomical and behavioral data. The general principle that leg neuropils control legs and tectulum controls wings (C70) is consistent with established knowledge. The broader hypothesis about tectulum involvement in complex coordination (C71-C72) is a reasonable inference from the data showing that walking-related hemilineages also project to tectulum.

results.result: Hemilineage 1A consists of projection neurons that cross the midline via the vA commissure, bifurcate into dorsal and ventral projections, and have primary outputs in the ventral leg neuropil. TRPA1 activation of 1A neurons evoked forward locomotion with intersegmental coordination but erratic leg movements lacking the normal tripod gait.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 describe the anatomy and function of hemilineage 1A. The anatomical description (C101-C103) is well-supported by Figure 4A-C, including nSyt::GFP localization showing output regions. The behavioral phenotype (C104-C105) is documented in Figure 4D and Video 2, showing clear forward locomotion with intersegmental coordination despite lacking normal gait patterns. The comparison to normal walking includes appropriate citation (Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990).

results.result: Hemilineage 2A neurons extend broadly within the ipsilateral tectulum. Activation of 2A interneurons drove high frequency wing movements in 54% of decapitated flies (n=25), with flies abruptly initiating flapping with wings in the flight position.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 describe hemilineage 2A anatomy and function. The anatomical description (C106) is supported by Figure 4G-I. The behavioral phenotype (C107-C108) includes quantitative data (54%, n=25) and is documented in Figure 4J and Video 3. The sample size is adequate for the behavioral characterization, and the phenotype is clearly distinct from other hemilineages.

results.result: Hemilineage 3A cell bodies remain ventral in the adult with arbors in intermediate leg neuropil. Hemilineage 3B is reduced/absent in T3 but in T1/T2 converges in the dorsal tectulum. Activation of 3B caused subtle leg repositioning, poorly coordinated movements, and occasional wing flicking but not high frequency buzzing.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 describe hemilineages 3A and 3B. The anatomical descriptions (C109-C111) are supported by Figure 4K-N. The behavioral phenotype for 3B (C112) is documented in Video 4. The 3A line had sensory contamination (C58) so behavioral data was appropriately not collected. The 3B behavioral phenotype is relatively subtle but clearly distinct from other hemilineages.

results.result: Hemilineage 5B cell bodies are pulled medially in the adult, with axons crossing in the iP commissure and forming a major ipsilateral arbor. Activation of 5B caused decapitated flies to progressively lower their body position, and tethered intact flies to crouch onto a ball they were holding.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 describe hemilineage 5B anatomy and function. The anatomical description (C113) is supported by Figure 4P-Q. The behavioral phenotypes (C114-C115) are documented in Figure 4R-S and Video 5, showing consistent postural changes in both decapitated and intact preparations. The use of both preparations strengthens the interpretation that 5B controls body position.

results.result: Hemilineage 6A is found in S3-A1, forms dorsalmost tectulum arbors with ipsilateral and converging contralateral projections. Hemilineage 6B is in T1-T3, crosses without ipsilateral arbor, and branches in tectulum and dorsal leg neuropils. Activation of 6A caused poorly coordinated leg movements pitching flies forward; 6B activation caused mixed leg movements with some forward movement or pivoting.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C122 describe hemilineages 6A and 6B. The anatomical descriptions (C116-C120) are well-supported by Figure 5A-F, including nSyt::GFP localization for 6A. The behavioral phenotypes (C121-C122) are documented in Figure 5G, 6D and Videos 6-7. Both hemilineages show leg-related behaviors consistent with their projections to leg neuropils and tectulum, though the movements are less coordinated than some other hemilineages.

results.result: Hemilineage 7B projects dorsally with ipsilateral tectulum arbor, crosses midline, and ascends through the neck connective, with prominent projections into T2 leg neuropil. Activation caused decapitated flies to abruptly launch into the air, with high-speed video confirming the normal takeoff sequence: wing raising, T2 leg extension (jump), then wing depression and flapping.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C126 describe hemilineage 7B anatomy and function. The anatomical description (C123-C124) is supported by Figure 5H-I. The takeoff behavior (C125-C126) is documented in Videos 8-9 and Figure 5J, with high-speed video confirming the behavioral sequence matches normal takeoff (citation to Card and Dickinson 2008). This is one of the most striking and well-characterized behavioral phenotypes in the study.

results.result: Hemilineage 8A neurons have arbors in lateral ipsilateral leg neuropil. Hemilineage 8B contains multi-part intersegmental arbors, including the T3 contralateral haltere interneurons (cHINs) with their distinctive bowtie arbor that receives haltere sensory input. Activation of 8A had minimal behavioral effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 describe hemilineages 8A and 8B. The anatomical descriptions (C127-C130) are well-supported by Figure 5K-O, with appropriate citation for the cHINs (Strausfeld and Seyan, 1985). The minimal behavioral effect of 8A activation (C131) is documented in Figure 5M and Video 10. The 8B line had contamination so behavioral data was appropriately not collected (C57-C58). The identification of cHINs as part of 8B is a valuable anatomical finding.

results.result: Hemilineage 9A neurons are local leg interneurons in the ventral leg neuropil that overlap with leg chordotonal organ afferents. Activation caused a subtle postural change with legs gradually splaying out during the heat ramp.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 describe hemilineage 9A anatomy and function. The anatomical description (C132-C133) is supported by Figure 5P-Q and citations to prior work (Brown and Truman 2009, Harris 2012). The behavioral phenotype (C134) is documented in Figure 5R and Video 11. The subtle postural change is consistent with the anatomy showing overlap with proprioceptive afferents, suggesting a role in posture control.

results.result: Hemilineage 10B cell bodies remain anteromedial, with neurites crossing in an iA bundle to form ventral and dorsal arbors. Activation caused leg movements that were erratic and often caused pivoting, with net movement usually backwards when it occurred.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 describe hemilineage 10B anatomy and function. The anatomical description (C135) is supported by Figure 6A-B. The behavioral phenotype (C136) is documented in Figure 6C and Video 12, showing clear leg movements with backward bias. The erratic nature and backward movement distinguish this from the forward-biased 1A phenotype.

results.result: Lineages 11A (T1-T2) and 11B (T2 only) have complex projections predominantly in T2 tectulum. Activation evoked takeoff behavior, but with altered sequencing compared to normal takeoff (wing flapping before jump). Using tsh-GAL80 to suppress thoracic expression while maintaining descending neuron expression severely reduced takeoffs (9% vs 100%), confirming thoracic lineage 11 drives the behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C141 describe lineages 11A/B anatomy and function. The anatomical description (C137-C138) is supported by Figure 6D-E. The takeoff behavior (C139-C140) is documented in Figure 6F and Video 13. Critically, the tsh-GAL80 experiment (C141) provides strong evidence that thoracic neurons, not descending neurons, drive the behavior. The altered behavioral sequence compared to 7B and normal takeoff is an interesting difference suggesting distinct circuit mechanisms.

results.result: Hemilineage 12A arborizes throughout dorsal tectulum with T1/T2 convergence. Activation produced a behavioral sequence: walking, then wing flicking and lateral wing vibration (resembling courtship song), then extreme frequency wing vibrations. Hemilineage 12B crosses to contralateral leg neuropil; activation caused tonic leg extension and freezing in some flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 describe hemilineages 12A and 12B. The anatomical descriptions (C142-C144) are supported by Figure 6G-L, including nSyt::GFP localization. The 12A behavioral sequence (C145) is well-documented in Figure 6J and Video 14, showing clear progression through different behaviors. The 12B phenotype (C146) is documented in Figure 6M-N and Video 15. The 12A sequence is one of the clearest examples of sequential rather than tonic behavioral responses.

results.result: Hemilineage 13A neurons insert near the leg nerve and ramify through ventral leg neuropil. Hemilineage 13B cell bodies are pulled medially, cross in the vA commissure as the ventral-most bundle, and branch through ventral leg neuropil. Activation of 13B caused tonic postural change with progressive leg extension to the side, often ending with flies resting on coxae with tarsi elevated.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C150 describe hemilineages 13A and 13B. The anatomical descriptions (C147-C149) are supported by Figure 6O-R. The 13B behavioral phenotype (C150) is documented in Figure 6S-T and Video 16. No behavioral data for 13A due to line quality (C58). The 13B phenotype is a clear tonic postural change distinct from other leg-related hemilineages.

results.result: In lineage 14, most 14B neurons die, leaving the cluster almost exclusively 14A neurons. During metamorphosis, 14A cell clusters are pulled to the anterior midline, and neurons arborize throughout ventral leg neuropil and laterally where motoneurons arborize.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C153 describe hemilineage 14A anatomy. The developmental observation (C151) is supported by citation (Truman et al. 2010). The anatomical description (C152-C153) is supported by Figure 6U-V. No behavioral data due to line contamination (C58). The anatomical characterization is valuable despite lack of behavioral data.

results.result: Hemilineage 15B is a major leg motoneuron lineage supplying distal leg muscles. Hemilineage 18B (missing from T1, present in T2-T3) has complex tectulum projections with T2 concentration in dorsal tectulum and ventral projections to leg neuropils. Activation of 18B caused walking sometimes with jerky wing movements, followed by jumping and transition to flapping (not always in that order).
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C159 describe hemilineages 15B and 18B. The 15B characterization (C154-C155) is supported by Figure 7A-B and citations to prior detailed work. No behavioral data for 15B due to line contamination. The 18B anatomy (C156-C158) is supported by Figure 7C-D. The 18B behavioral phenotype (C159) is documented in Figure 7E and Video 17, showing a complex sequence involving both legs and wings consistent with projections to both leg and tectulum neuropils.

results.result: Hemilineage 19A projects to ipsilateral leg neuropil with medial projections from T1-T2 converging at T2 midline (nSyt::GFP localizes to distal medial projection). Hemilineage 19B (reduced in T1, small in T3) makes robust T2 projection across iP commissure to dorsal tectulum. Activation of 19A caused flies to stay in place with incessant T2 leg waving but no T1/T3 leg movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C165 describe hemilineages 19A and 19B. The anatomical descriptions (C160-C164) are supported by Figure 7F-K and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, including nSyt::GFP localization. The 19A behavioral phenotype (C165) is documented in Figure 7I and Video 18, showing striking segment-specific leg movements. No behavioral data for 19B due to sensory contamination. The 19A phenotype is one of the most segment-specific behaviors observed.

results.result: Hemilineages 20A and 22A are adjoining lineages whose A progeny project to ventral leg neuropil and are difficult to distinguish. In the adult, 20A/22A clusters project to mid leg neuropil with lateral and medial branches. Activation caused simple postural change with progressive leg extension into a splayed posture.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C169 describe hemilineages 20A/22A. The developmental observation (C166) is supported by citation. The anatomical descriptions (C167-C168) are supported by Figure 7L-M. The behavioral phenotype (C169) is documented in Figure 7N and Video 19. The inability to distinguish 20A from 22A is a limitation but is clearly acknowledged. The simple postural phenotype is consistent with leg neuropil projections.

results.result: Hemilineage 21A neurons remain close to 20A/22A cells and project through most of the ipsilateral leg neuropil. Activation induced uncoordinated leg movements lacking both intralimb and interlimb coordination, with incessant movements but flies typically not moving from their place.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C171 describe hemilineage 21A anatomy and function. The anatomical description (C170) is supported by Figure 7O-P. The behavioral phenotype (C171) is documented in Figure 7Q and Video 20. The lack of coordination distinguishes this from other leg-related hemilineages like 1A that show intersegmental coordination.

results.result: Only hemilineage 23B survives in lineage 23. Cell bodies are ventrolateral in larva but displaced dorsally during metamorphosis. Adult 23B neurons project ventrally, cross the iP commissure with robust ipsilateral arbor in ventralmost leg neuropil overlapping with leg sensory neurons. Activation caused progressive higher frequency intersegmental limb movements but poor intralimb coordination.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C176 describe hemilineage 23B. The developmental observation (C172) is supported by citation. The anatomical descriptions (C173-C175) are supported by Figure 7R-S. The behavioral phenotype (C176) is documented in Figure 7T and Video 21. The overlap with sensory neurons (C175) is consistent with the behavioral phenotype showing limb movements, and the poor intralimb coordination distinguishes this from more coordinated hemilineages.

results.result: Hemilineage 24B is a motor lineage (smaller than 15B) innervating proximal leg muscles, with dendrites in intermediate leg neuropil. Stimulation produced repetitive leg movements typically without net movement, with legs often held at awkward angles by the end of the ramp.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C180 describe hemilineage 24B. The characterization as a motor lineage (C177-C179) is supported by Figure 7U-V and citations to prior detailed work (Baek and Mann 2009, Brierley et al. 2012). The behavioral phenotype (C180) is documented in Figure 7W and Video 22. The repetitive movements without net displacement are consistent with direct motoneuron activation.

results.result: The vPR6 neurons (required for male courtship song) are part of hemilineage 12A. Using hemilineage 12A drivers with fruP1.LexA reliably captured approximately 12 cells in males and 3-5 in females, with arbor shape matching the digitally masked vPR6 cluster. This demonstrates that the toolkit can identify developmental origins and genetically isolate specific neuronal populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C185 demonstrate the utility of the hemilineage toolkit. The vPR6 characterization (C181) is supported by citation (Yu et al. 2010b). The anatomical inference (C182) is reasonable based on location and projections. The genetic isolation (C183-C184) is documented in Figure 8 with appropriate citations for methods. This proof-of-principle demonstration (C185) is valuable for showing how the toolkit can be applied to dissect specific functional populations.

results.result: Hemilineages have modular function with cells in a given group associated with particular behavioral responses. This organization is consistent with physiological data from grasshoppers showing computational circuits built from lineage-related interneuron clusters, and with vertebrate spinal cord organization where cell types from defined precursors play specific roles in circuit motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 synthesize the findings and place them in comparative context. The modular function conclusion (C73) is well-supported by the comprehensive anatomical and behavioral data across hemilineages. The comparisons to grasshoppers (C74) and vertebrates (C75) are supported by appropriate citations (Burrows 1996, Shepherd and Laurent 1992, Grillner and Jessell 2009) and provide valuable evolutionary and comparative perspective.

results.result: The vPR6 neurons required for male courtship song are part of hemilineage 12A. Most hemilineage lines had some contamination with off-target expression, and lines with sensory neuron expression or other hemilineage contamination were not used for behavioral studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C58 address important caveats. The vPR6 identification (C76) is supported by Figure 7 and citation, highlighting that hemilineages can contain functionally specialized subpopulations. The acknowledgment of contamination (C57-C58) is important for interpreting the behavioral data and shows appropriate experimental rigor in excluding problematic lines. These caveats are essential for proper interpretation of the results.

results.result: Decapitated flies were used for behavioral testing because they maintain good stance with little spontaneous movement except grooming. Control flies lacking TRPA1 showed no response to heat ramps. TRPA1 shows activity at 25°C and is fully active at 27-32°C.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C188 describe the experimental system. The use of decapitated flies (C186) is justified by their stable baseline behavior documented in Video 1. The control experiment (C187) is essential for validating the approach. The TRPA1 properties (C188) are supported by citation (Hamada et al. 2008). These methodological details are important for interpreting the behavioral results.

results.result: The insect segmental CNS provides an unparalleled system for studying nervous system evolution due to the stereotyped array of segmental NBs that has changed little through insect evolution. Homologous stem cells can be identified across diverse insects based on position, molecular markers, and early progeny. Early-born primary neurons have conserved identities determined by birth-order, while later-born secondary neurons are born after grainyhead expression begins.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 provide evolutionary context. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to prior comparative work (Thomas et al. 1984, Truman and Ball 1998, Isshiki et al. 2001, Almeida and Bray 2005, Zhou et al. 2009). The distinction between primary and secondary neurons is important for understanding the scope of the current study (which focuses on secondary neurons). This background is essential for appreciating the evolutionary significance of the findings.

results.result: Conservation of hemilineage properties across insects is illustrated by the medial lineage, where A hemilineage cells are GABAergic engrailed-positive local interneurons and B cells are engrailed-negative projection cells in both grasshoppers and Drosophila. Comparative analysis of GABA-immunoreactive neurons supports conservation of hemilineage properties across insects, though individual neurons within a class likely cannot be homologized.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 discuss evolutionary conservation. The medial lineage example (C84-C85) is supported by citation for grasshoppers (Jia and Siegler 2002) and unpublished data for Drosophila. The broader conservation argument (C86) is supported by citation (Witten and Truman 1998). The caveat about individual neuron homology (C87) is explicitly speculative but reasonable given the numbers of neurons involved. This discussion appropriately balances evidence for conservation at the class level with uncertainty at the individual neuron level.

results.result: Functional conservation of hemilineages across insects is supported by examples: grasshopper ventral interneurons in the transverse tract receive wing afferent input while fly 2A interneurons (main transverse tract neurons) drive flight; grasshopper NB4-1 and NB3-1 make leg circuit interneurons while homologous fly NBs generate similar-appearing leg neuropil interneurons (14A and 4B). The authors expect functional roles of most hemilineages to be highly conserved through insect evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 provide specific examples of functional conservation supported by citations and the current study's data. However, C92 is explicitly an expectation/speculation about broad conservation. While the examples support the possibility of conservation, comprehensive functional characterization across species would be needed to confirm this expectation. The speculation is reasonable but goes beyond the current evidence.

results.result: For simpler hemilineages with parallel units, changes in neuron numbers could alter functionality by changing spatial/temporal resolution, potentially providing finer control over locomotion speed (as seen in zebrafish). For complex hemilineages, changes in neuronal properties/connectivity rather than numbers might be more important for behavioral evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are explicitly speculative about evolutionary mechanisms. C94 is supported by citation to zebrafish work (McLean et al. 2008) showing a relevant example, but C93 and C95 are hypotheses about how hemilineage evolution might occur. These are reasonable speculations based on the anatomical diversity observed, but would require comparative studies across species with different behaviors to test directly.

results.result: Important caveats for interpreting the results: Drosophila's flight system (mesothoracic wings, metathoracic halteres) is highly derived compared to basal insects; about a third of thoracic hemilineages die in flies; some ancestral cell types may have been lost; the analysis includes only postembryonic secondary neurons, lacking embryonic-born neurons. A thoracic unit has about 2500 pairs of neurons, most assignable to 33 hemilineage units.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 provide important caveats for interpretation. The derived nature of Drosophila flight (C96) is based on established knowledge. The hemilineage death (C97) is supported by citation (Truman et al. 2010). The inference about lost cell types (C98) is reasonable given C96-C97. The limitation to postembryonic neurons (C99) is clearly stated. The quantitative statement (C100) summarizes the scope. These caveats are essential for proper interpretation and show appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The 33 postembryonically-born hemilineages contribute over 90% of thoracic hemisegment neurons. Activation of hemilineages elicited behaviors of increasing complexity: simplest hemilineages (local interneurons) caused tonic/phasic leg movements lacking interlimb coordination; intermediate hemilineages (projection cells) drove intersegmentally coordinated behaviors like walking; highest level hemilineages elicited complex behaviors like takeoff.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5 summarize the main findings from the abstract. C2 is a quantitative statement supported by the anatomical analysis. C3-C5 describe the hierarchical organization of behavioral complexity, which is well-supported by the comprehensive behavioral characterization across hemilineages (Figures 4-9). The correlation between hemilineage anatomy (local vs. projection) and behavioral complexity (simple vs. complex) is a major finding of the study.

results.result: Background on nervous system organization: Drosophila CNS has ~100,000 neurons each capable of dozens of synaptic connections. In vertebrate spinal cord, identified progenitors generate interneuron pools with defined circuit roles, with functional organization conserved from fish to mammals. Similarly, insect VNS is the site of sensorimotor patterning for complex behaviors, with specific NBs generating functionally similar interneuron pools. The insect VNS develops from a conserved segmental set of 30 paired + 1 unpaired NBs. With flight evolution, thoracic neuron numbers doubled through extended NB proliferation rather than adding new NBs.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C16 provide essential background context. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Power 1943, Chiang et al. 2011, Grillner and Jessell 2009, Lupo et al. 2006, Shepherd and Laurent 1992, Thompson and Siegler 1991, Thomas et al. 1984, Truman and Ball 1998, Broadus and Doe 1995, Bossing et al. 1996, Schmid et al. 1999). This background establishes the rationale for the study and places it in the context of comparative neuroscience.

results.result: Hemilineages are units of early molecular diversity: many early transcription factors are restricted along hemilineage lines, and many have homologs involved in vertebrate spinal cord fate determination. For example, Dbx1 controls V0/V1 fate differences in mouse spinal cord, while Drosophila dbx controls VNS cell type differentiation through interactions with even-skipped and hb9.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 establish the molecular basis for hemilineage identity. These claims are well-supported by citations to published work (Lacin et al. 2014, Thor and Thomas 1997, Pierani et al. 2001, Lacin et al. 2009). The parallel between Drosophila and vertebrate transcription factor roles provides important evolutionary context and suggests deep conservation of developmental mechanisms.

results.result: Four hemilineages (0A, 4A, 16B, 17A) were not addressed in this study.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 clearly states the scope limitation. This is a straightforward statement about which hemilineages were not studied, important for understanding the completeness of the coverage.
